title: Data Center Is Fined $1.1 Million for Operating 62 Power Generators

reading.body:
This is a compliance failure in the physical infrastructure of a data center deployment, not a failure of an AI model or of automated decision-making. The generators that supply power to the Vineland site were installed and operated before the required permits were obtained, and state inspectors found them in that condition in late July. The failure sits at the point where a facility is energized and run, which is downstream of site planning and upstream of any computing workload the campus would host.

Catching it would have required a permit check before the generators were installed and again before they were run. The reporting describes detection by state inspectors rather than by the operator, so no internal control is shown to have flagged the gap. Because the campus is partly in use and scheduled for completion at the end of the year, the equipment was already serving an operating facility when the violation was recorded.

What is not established is fault beyond the penalty itself. The federal lawsuit from homeowners over noise is an allegation and not a finding, the Cumberland County Health Department orders concern noise rather than the air permits, and the reporting does not establish intent to operate without permits. The reporting also does not describe any AI system as the cause of the violation.

reports.title: Data Center Is Fined $1.1 Million for Operating 62 Power Generators

summary:
New Jersey fined DataOne $1.07 million after state inspectors found 62 natural-gas generators at its Vineland data center site in late July. The 2,000-kilowatt generators, each about the size of a tractor-trailer, lacked required permits to be installed or operated. Officials said the penalty for violating the Air Pollution Control Act was the largest ever issued to a data center operator in New Jersey. The fine was announced Tuesday.

The planned data center is a 2.6 million-square-foot campus that would need 350 megawatts, enough to power a medium-size city, and is scheduled for completion at the end of the year. Some of it is already in use. It has drawn complaints, including a federal lawsuit from homeowners over persistent noise and violation orders from the Cumberland County Health Department for excessive noise. Governor Mikie Sherrill said at a Climate Week event that building such projects must benefit New Jersey communities.
